tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

return started >= str_to_dt(enqueued_at) and ended >= started


def _execute_crawl_task(
    self,
    connection_row,
    org_row,
    function_name,
    first_crawl,
    start_time_str,
    end_time_str,
    page_token,
    force=False,
    local_submit=False,
    no_heartbeat=False,
    protected=False,
    sync_job_id=None,
):
    # ecs agent should reject celery tasks when scale-in event is received
    if shutdown_requested:
        logger.info("shutdown requested - rejecting new crawl task")
        raise self.reject(requeue=True)

    connection_id = connection_row["id"]
    integration_secret = connection_row["integration_secret"]
    integration_name = connection_row["integration_name"]
    created_at = connection_row["created_at"]
    integration_type = connection_row["integration_type"]
    org_id = org_row["id"]
    org_name = org_row["name"]

    if sync_job_id:
        # synced crawl - check sync job status
        row_to_check = get_sync_job(sync_job_id)
        if not row_to_check:
            logger.error(f"Sync job {sync_job_id} not found")
            return
        if row_to_check["status"] != "open":
            logger.info(
                f"Sync job {sync_job_id} is no longer open (status: {row_to_check['status']})"
            )
            return
    else:
        # regular crawl - check scheduler row
        row_to_check = get_scheduler_row(connection_id, function_name)

    stale = row_to_check.get("stale", False)
    paused = row_to_check.get("paused", False)
    force_sync_pending = bool(row_to_check.get("force_sync_pending"))
    if crawl_heartbeat_active(row_to_check) and crawl_started(row_to_check):
        logger.info(
            f"Crawl task {function_name} for connection {connection_id} is already running"
        )
        if not DRY_RUN:
            if force:
                # force overrides the already-running guard. prompt only when a human is
                # driving; a worker has no stdin, so input() there raises EOFError and kills
                # the crawl instead of honoring the explicit force.
                if sys.stdin and sys.stdin.isatty():
                    to_continue = input(
                        "Crawl is already running. Do you want to continue? (y/n): "
                    )
                    if to_continue.lower() != "y":
                        logger.info("Exiting crawl task")
                        return
            else:
                return
    # a dead worker's crawl comes back from both sqs and the scheduler. once one
    # copy has finished, the other would only crawl the same window again
    regular_crawl = not sync_job_id and not force and not force_sync_pending
    if regular_crawl and crawl_superseded(
        message_enqueued_at(self.request), row_to_check
    ):
        logger.info(
            f"Crawl task {function_name} for connection {connection_id} already "
            "ran again since this copy was queued, skipping"
        )
        return

    try:
        org_private_key = get_org_private_key(org_id)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Error getting org private key: {format_exception(e)}")
        raise Exception(f"org private key not found for {org_id}")
    try:
        integration_secret = org_decrypt(integration_secret, org_private_key)
    except Exception:
        raise Exception("integration secret could not be decoded")

    integration = build_integration(
        connection_row, org_id, integration_secret=integration_secret
    )
    # log crawl id for browserbase tracking
    crawl_id = integration.crawl_id
    logger.updateConfig({"crawl_id": crawl_id})
    if force_sync_pending:
        logger.updateConfig({"force_sync_pending": True, "paused": paused})
    else:
        logger.deleteConfig("force_sync_pending")
        logger.deleteConfig("paused")
    if sync_job_id:
        logger.updateConfig({"sync_job_id": sync_job_id})
    else:
        logger.deleteConfig("sync_job_id")
    tracer.set_tag("crawl_id", crawl_id)
    resource = function_to_resource_map[integration_type][function_name](integration)

    crawl_frequency = resolve_crawl_frequency(
        connection_row, org_row, resource, function_name
    )
    due = True
    if not sync_job_id:
        due = crawl_due(row_to_check, crawl_frequency)
    if force or force_sync_pending:
        pass
    elif not due and row_to_check.get("last_crawl_end"):
        logger.info(
            f"Crawl task {function_name} for connection {connection_id} is not due"
        )
        if not DRY_RUN:
            return

    # start_time_str will be None if it's first crawl and it's never been started before.
    # if it has been started before, first_crawl will be True but start_time_str will have a value.
    # it might have latest_data too.
    if first_crawl and not start_time_str:  # always False for sync jobs
        first_crawl_lookback_days = get_first_crawl_lookback_days(
            org_row, integration_type
        )
        if (
            org_id in INTEGRATION_SPECIFIC_LOOKBACK_DAYS_ORGS
            and integration_name in INTEGRATION_SPECIFIC_LOOKBACK_DAYS_ORGS[org_id]
            and function_name
            in INTEGRATION_SPECIFIC_LOOKBACK_DAYS_ORGS[org_id][integration_name]
        ):
            first_crawl_lookback_days = INTEGRATION_SPECIFIC_LOOKBACK_DAYS_ORGS[org_id][
                integration_name
            ][function_name]
        start_time_str = dt_to_str(
            str_to_dt(created_at) - timedelta(days=first_crawl_lookback_days)
        )
        logger.updateConfig({"start_time": f"{start_time_str} (first crawl)"})
    if not start_time_str:  # always present for sync jobs
        start_time_str = created_at
    if not end_time_str:  # always present for sync jobs
        end_time_str = dt_to_str(now())
        logger.updateConfig({"end_time": f"{end_time_str} (none)"})
    start_time_dt = str_to_dt(start_time_str) - timedelta(
        minutes=integration.crawl_start_overlap_minutes
    )
    end_time_dt = str_to_dt(end_time_str)
    logger.info(f"Starting crawl from {start_time_str} to {end_time_str}")

                worker_hostname,
                stop_event,
                connection_id,
                function_name,

                rsp, child_resource_rsp, page_submit_task_ids = get_and_submit(
                    resource,
                    start_time_dt,
                    end_time_dt,
                    first_crawl,
                    first_loop,

                else:

                            deferred_page_token or next_token
                        )

                            update_items["current_crawl_end"] = None

                logger.info(
                    f"Wrote {len(data)} items to submitter lambda s3 for table {table_name}: page {page}"
                )

        # check that crawl/sync jobs are complete and send relevant webhooks
        if sync_job_id:
            update_sync_job_rsp = update_sync_job(
                sync_job_id,
                {
                    "last_crawl_end": current_time,

                        resource, start_time_str, end_time_str, crawl_id

                    update_crawl_items(
                        resource.integration.connection_id,
                        function_name,
                        {"force_sync_pending": False},

        logger.info("Stopping heartbeat thread")
        stop_event.set()
        heartbeat_thread.join()

        ecs_task_protection_request(False, connection_row, function_name)

content.text:
You're right about the first one. The second is fine in your exact scenario, but it does break once a crawl has moved its window forward.

**1. `next_start` is checked against 9 AM, but the integration was asked for data from 8 AM.** The check is `current_start_dt < next_start <= end_time_dt` (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:474`), with `current_start_dt` set to the 9 AM start before the overlap is subtracted (`:386`). The integration only sees `start` = 8 AM. If its natural cursor lands between 8 and 9 (say the last row on a page is 8:30), the crawl stops with a 500. It fails loudly rather than losing data, but the integration has to know about a start time it was never given.

ShipStation already works around this. It rebuilds `start_without_overlap` on the first loop and falls back to a page token when the cursor is at or before it (`integrations/wms/shipstation/integration.py:361-414`).

There is a reason to keep 9 AM as the lower bound: a `next_start` of 8:30 becomes `set_latest_data`, which would move `latest_data` backwards. So the fix isn't simply to compare against 8 AM. Two cleaner options:
- Clamp in the crawler: accept anything above `start_time_dt` and only advance the window when `next_start > current_start_dt`.
- Pass the start without the overlap to the integration so it can make that call itself.

**2. Resuming with a page token.** In your exact case it's fine. The first run queries from 8 AM. When page 3 fails, `current_crawl_start` holds 9 AM, the value before the overlap (`:547`). On resume, 9 AM minus 60 minutes is 8 AM again, so the query matches the one that produced the token.

It breaks after a `next_start`:
1. Page 1 returns `next_start` = 10 AM, so `start_time_dt` becomes 10 AM with no overlap (`:557-558`).
2. Once the submits drain, `advance_latest_data` sets `current_crawl_start` = 10 AM (`lambda_handlers/submitter.py:198`).
3. Page 2 of the 10 AM window stores a token, then page 3 fails.
4. On resume, the scheduler passes 10 AM (`lambda_handlers/scheduler.py:117`) and the crawler subtracts the overlap again, giving 9 AM. The token came from a query that started at 10 AM.

Without `store_current_crawl_params`, the same thing happens through `latest_data`.

How much that hurts depends on the cursor:
- **Keyset tokens** that carry their own position (ShipStation's `{modify_date, page}`) ignore the start, so there's no harm.
- **Offset or page-number** pagination returns a different slice of a wider query, so rows get duplicated or skipped.
- **Opaque vendor cursors** tied to the original filters may error or quietly return the wrong page.

Simplest fix for #2: when a page token is present, skip the overlap. Resuming a cursor is by definition continuing an existing query, not starting a new window:

```python
overlap = timedelta(minutes=integration.crawl_start_overlap_minutes)
if page_token:
    overlap = timedelta(0)
start_time_dt = str_to_dt(start_time_str) - overlap
```

That breaks your exact scenario, though. There the token came from the first query, which did include the overlap, so skipping it on resume would re-query from 9 AM against a token built at 8 AM. To handle both cases, store the actual query start (`start_time_dt`) as `current_crawl_start` whenever a token is saved, and never subtract the overlap from a `current_crawl_start`. I can make that change if you want. It touches `crawler.py`, `scheduler.py` and `advance_latest_data`.

    store_crawl_params_connection_row,
    org_row,
    store_crawl_params_resource,
    now_mock,
    update_crawl_items_mock,
    mocker,
):
    # a window that ends early advances latest_data to its own end and the crawl keeps
    # going from there, instead of the integration hiding the rest of the range in a token
    start_time_str = "2019-12-01T00:00:00Z"
    end_time_str = dt_to_str(now_mock.return_value)
    next_start = str_to_dt("2019-12-16T00:00:00Z")
    starts_seen = []

    def side_effect(
        resource,
        start,
        end,
        first_crawl,
        first_loop,
        page_token,
        local_submit,
        sync_job_id=None,
        notify_force_sync=False,
    ):
        starts_seen.append(start)
        if first_loop:
            page = {"next_token": None, "data": [], "next_start": next_start}
            return page, {}, {"submit_task_id_1"}
        return {"next_token": None, "data": []}, {}, {"submit_task_id_2"}

    mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.get_and_submit", side_effect=side_effect)
    wait_mock = mocker.patch("celery_tasks.crawler.wait_for_submit_drain")

    crawler.crawl_task(
        store_crawl_params_connection_row,
        org_row,
        "get_bills",
        False,
        start_time_str,
        end_time_str,
        None,
    )

    integration = store_crawl_params_resource.integration
    overlap = timedelta(minutes=integration.crawl_start_overlap_minutes)
    assert starts_seen == [
        str_to_dt(start_time_str) - overlap,
        next_start,
    ]
    wait_mock.assert_called_once_with(
        store_crawl_params_connection_row["id"],
        "get_bills",
        dt_to_str(next_start),
        sync_job_id=None,
    )

    window_calls = []
    final_calls = []
    for call_elem in update_crawl_items_mock.call_args_list:
        submit = call_elem[0][2].get("submit", {})
        if submit.get("set_latest_data") == dt_to_str(next_start):
            window_calls.append(call_elem[0][2])
        elif submit.get("set_latest_data") == end_time_str:
            final_calls.append(call_elem[0][2])

    assert len(window_calls) == 1
    window_update = window_calls[0]
    assert window_update["submit"]["mark_complete"] is False
    # the end is pinned here, but the start only moves once the rows have landed, so
    # the crawler must not write it alongside the arm
    assert "current_crawl_start" not in window_update

    # the window is fully drained, so there is no in-window token to resume from
    assert window_update["latest_page_token"] is None

    assert len(final_calls) == 1
    assert final_calls[0]["submit"]["mark_complete"] is True

crawler: check next_start against the start the integration was given

The crawler passed the integration the start with the overlap but checked next_start
against the start without it, so a next_start inside the overlap failed the crawl.
latest_data is clamped to the crawl's raw start so it never moves back. Drops the
shipstation workaround that recomputed the start without the overlap.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01PKbHKDKFv2Zx2QZ44FRumt
EOF
git push -q -u origin better-crawler-names 2>&1 | tail -2
sed -n '/<!-- ship-on-merge -->/,/<!-- \/ship-on-merge -->/p' .github/pull_request_template.md > "$TMPDIR/ship.md"
cat > "$TMPDIR/body.md" <<'EOF'
The crawler checked `next_start` against the start without the overlap, but the integration only ever sees the start with it. A `next_start` inside the overlap (say 8:30 for a 9:00 crawl with a 60 minute overlap) failed the crawl with a 500.

`next_start` is now checked against the start the integration was actually given. The written `latest_data` is clamped to the crawl's raw start, so a `next_start` inside the overlap moves the window without moving `latest_data` backwards.

- `celery_tasks/crawler.py`: `raw_start_str`/`raw_start_dt` hold the start from the scheduler. `start_time_str`/`start_time_dt` are the overlapped start the loop begins from. `current_start_dt` is the one the loop moves forward. `current_crawl_start` still stores the raw start, so resuming works the same as before.
- ShipStation `get_orders`: removed `start_without_overlap`, which recomputed the raw start to satisfy the old check.
- Linked refresh now gets the crawl's full range instead of the last window's start.
- New test: a `next_start` inside the overlap moves the window and keeps `latest_data` at the raw start.

Verified with a compile and format check only. Local tests can't reach the dev database from this machine (the same errors happen on `main`), so CI runs the full suite.

test override: `yarn test`

content.text:
I opened https://github.com/trackstarhq/pokedex/pull/6292, but none of the tests have run yet. Tests can't reach the dev database from this machine (the same setup errors happen on `main`, probably the VPN), so I only checked that the files compile and are formatted. The PR runs the full suite with `test override: yarn test`.

**Naming** (`celery_tasks/crawler.py`):
- `raw_start_str` / `raw_start_dt` hold the start the scheduler passes in.
- `start_time_str` / `start_time_dt` are now the same value (the raw start minus the overlap), and that's where the loop starts.
- `current_start_dt` starts at `start_time_dt` and is the only one that changes during the loop. It's what gets passed to `get_and_submit`.

**The fix:** `next_start` is now checked against `current_start_dt`, the start the integration was actually given. The one catch is that a `next_start` inside the overlap (say 8:30) would otherwise write `latest_data` earlier than the 9 AM it already was. So the value written to `latest_data`, and used for the submit-drain wait, is `max(next_start, raw_start_dt)`. The window still moves to 8:30, but `latest_data` stays at 9.

**Resuming is unchanged.** `current_crawl_start` still saves the raw start (`max(current_start_dt, raw_start_dt)`), because the scheduler subtracts the overlap again when it resumes. The window-moved resume bug from my last reply is still there.

**ShipStation:** I removed `start_without_overlap`. It now uses `start < last_second_dt < end` with the `start` it's passed. The `else` branch that pages on with a token is still needed, but for a different reason now: a `next_start` exactly at `end` would finish the crawl and drop any remaining orders in that second. I updated its comment to say so.

**Changes in behaviour:**
- Linked refresh used to get the start of the last window. It now gets the start of the whole crawl, which is what it should get since it collects IDs from every window.
- The force-sync webhook and the historical-sync record still report the raw start, as before.
- The "Starting crawl from" log line now shows the start with the overlap.

I added one test for a `next_start` inside the overlap: the window moves to it, and `latest_data` stays at the raw start.

content.text:
Mostly yes. The rule I'd use is narrower than "no overlap for `store_current_crawl_params`": a crawl that resumes from `current_crawl_start` shouldn't overlap. A crawl that starts fresh from `latest_data` should. For that to work, `current_crawl_start` has to store the start the query actually used, with the overlap already applied, as you said.

**Why this is right.** `current_crawl_start` is only set while a crawl is in progress, in two places:
- **Mid-window with a token** (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:537`). The token came from a query that started at `current_start_dt`, so resuming has to start there exactly. Storing the start with the overlap applied and not subtracting again gives exactly that.
- **After a `next_start` window drains** (`advance_latest_data`, `lambda_handlers/submitter.py:198`). Within a single run, the next window starts exactly at `next_start` with no overlap. A resume that also starts there matches what the run would have done.

Either way, resuming just continues the same crawl. The overlap is protection for the gap between two separate crawls, not for continuing one.

**Why not drop the overlap for these resources entirely.** Their fresh crawls start from `latest_data` like every other resource, and that's where the overlap catches records that show up late. WMS orders, products, inbounds and bills all store crawl params by default (`integrations/wms/WMSIntegration.py:160-164` and others), so dropping the overlap for them would remove it from most of the crawls it exists for.

**"Skip the overlap when a token is present" can't be the rule on its own**, because other resources store a token without crawl params: returns, inventory ledger, warehouses, carrier invoices. They resume from `latest_data` (9 AM), and their token came from the 8 AM query. That's your original case, and it's only correct today because the crawler subtracts the overlap again. Skipping it would cause the exact mismatch you were worried about. These resources can't hit the case where the window has moved, because `next_start` requires crawl params (`test_next_start_needs_somewhere_to_record_the_resume_point`). So leaving them as they are is correct.

**The complication is that the crawler can't tell where its start came from.** Only the scheduler knows whether it passed `current_crawl_start` or `latest_data` (`lambda_handlers/scheduler.py:115-118`). Options:
1. **(recommended)** The scheduler passes a `resuming` kwarg when it uses `current_crawl_start`, and the crawler skips the overlap when that's set. The change is explicit and stays small. Queued messages that don't have the kwarg keep today's behavior.
2. The crawler compares its start to `row_to_check["current_crawl_start"]`, the scheduler row it already reads. That needs no signature change, but it's an inferred check.

**Sync jobs have the same bug and aren't covered by either option.** They resume from `max(requested_start, latest_data)` with the stored token (`lambda_handlers/sync_job_scheduler.py:103`) and have no `current_crawl_start`. So once a `next_start` has moved the window, the overlap is subtracted from a start that never had it. Fixing that means storing the query start on the sync job row too.

Separately, with this change the clamp from #6292 means that when a `next_start` lands inside the overlap, a resume would start at 9 AM rather than 8:30. That's safe because the previous crawl already covered everything before 9 AM.

Do you want this added to #6292, or as a separate PR? I'd keep it separate, since it changes resume behavior for every WMS orders crawl.

Paused 2026-09-30, after PR #6292 (next_start checked against the start the integration was given). User will ask "what still needs to be done" and this is the answer.

**Bug:** celery_tasks/crawler.py always subtracts crawl_start_overlap_minutes from the start it's given. When the scheduler resumes from current_crawl_start (lambda_handlers/scheduler.py ~115-118) after a next_start moved the window, the token came from a query starting at next_start (no overlap), but the resume queries from next_start minus overlap. Offset/opaque cursors then return the wrong page.

**Agreed direction:**
- current_crawl_start stores the actual query start (overlap applied), not the raw start.
- A resume from current_crawl_start never re-applies the overlap (it continues an in-progress crawl; in-run windows don't overlap either). Fresh crawls from latest_data keep the overlap.

- Crawler can't tell where its start came from. Recommended: scheduler passes a `resuming` kwarg when it uses current_crawl_start (old queued messages keep today's behavior). Alt: compare to row_to_check["current_crawl_start"].
- Sync jobs have the same bug: they resume from max(requested_start, latest_data) with the token (lambda_handlers/sync_job_scheduler.py ~103) and have no current_crawl_start; needs the query start stored on the sync job row.
- Recommended as a separate PR from #6292 (changes resume for every WMS orders crawl).

content.text:
The Greptile comment is technically right, but it only exists because of `latest_data_dt`. I agree that variable shouldn't be there.

**Greptile's point.** When `next_start` lands inside the overlap, the clamp makes `latest_data_dt` equal to `raw_start_dt`, which is already the row's `latest_data`. `wait_for_submit_drain` returns as soon as `row["latest_data"] == next_start` (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:123`), so it returns straight away without waiting for this window's submits.

It's less dangerous than Greptile says. `latest_data` doesn't move, and the next window's drain waits on the combined `tasks_started` set, so nothing moves past rows that haven't landed yet. But the drain is being skipped by accident, which is a bad sign.

**Why the clamp is wrong.** I added it so `latest_data` would never move backwards (9 AM → 8:30). That isn't worth protecting:
- Moving `latest_data` to 8:30 just means the next crawl starts from 8:30 minus the overlap, re-reading about half an hour. Upserts make that harmless.
- The value is correct: 8:30 is exactly how far this crawl has confirmed.
- If `set_latest_data` = `next_start` again, `latest_data` changes (8:30 ≠ 9:00), so the drain waits properly and Greptile's issue goes away.

The one thing that reads `latest_data` as a floor is `first_crawl_complete` (`utils/boto.py:1846`, `latest_data >= created_at`). A backwards step could only flip that on a connection less than one overlap old that has no `historical_sync_completed` flag. That's small enough to ignore.

So the fix is to delete `latest_data_dt` and go back to writing and draining on `next_start`, as `main` does. The comparison to `raw_start_dt` is then gone from that path.

The other place `raw_start_dt` is compared is `current_crawl_start = max(current_start_dt, raw_start_dt)`. That one has to stay for now: without it the first window would store 8 AM, and a resume would subtract the overlap again (7 AM). It goes away with the resume-overlap follow-up, which I've saved for when you ask what's left.

I'll remove `latest_data_dt` and update the test (`latest_data_writes == [dt_to_str(next_start), end_time_str]`, drain called with `next_start`) if you want. The CI failures on #6292 are all live vendor tests (i-fulfilment timeouts, oia-global, tps, mabang, ffe), not crawler tests.

# Code style (pokedex Python)

The always-on subset, consolidated from CLAUDE.md and `integration-patterns.md` "Code style". Full reviewer checklist (incl. advisory / new-build-only items like `while True`, guard clauses, inline dict values): `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Code style".

- **No docstrings, with two exceptions.** Pokedex code is self-documenting. Both exceptions are where the docstring is published text, not a comment: `api.py` endpoint handlers, whose docstring is the endpoint's OpenAPI summary and description (the rollout pushes that spec to Mintlify and Svix, so it is the public API docs, and every public endpoint carries one); Alembic migration modules under `migrations/versions/`, which keep the generated header (title, `Revision ID`, `Revises`, `Create Date`) plus a line of rationale when the schema change is not obvious from the operations. Nothing under `integrations/`, `utils/`, `resources/`, or `actions/` has one.
- **Default to no comment; when in doubt, delete.** A comment exists only when the change is not obvious from the code alone. If the code, a variable name, or the error message beside it already says it, the comment is noise — delete it rather than polish it. That covers narration ("sum the quantities per sku"), section labels, and anything restating an assert or a raise.
- **Comments: lowercase, ≤2 lines, why not what.** Vendor quirks, surprising invariants, non-obvious couplings. Vendor field names keep their original casing inside a lowercase comment (`DeliveryNotes` stays `DeliveryNotes`) — lowercasing them breaks the reference. The ceiling yields only when a genuinely non-obvious vendor data model or a disambiguating example needs the room and nothing shorter carries it. The same ceiling applies to raised error messages — a `PokedexException` says what went wrong and what to do in a line or two, not a paragraph.
- **ELI5, no jargon.** Write it the way you'd say it out loud to an engineer new to the codebase: plain words any SWE understands cold, in one read. No noun-stacks ("multi-lot pick collision"), no arrow chains (`x → y → z`), no model-speak ("ensure correctness", "for clarity", "leverage"), no clever compression that needs decoding ("must not look like it did"). "with no batch number, picks from different batches get combined here, so we can't keep a single expiry date" beats "blank-batch multi-lot picks collapse under the package uniqueness key, dropping the expiry anchor".
- **Comments are self-contained.** Never reference `api-summary.md`, any `.claude/...` file, doctrine vocabulary ("tier-3", "shallow-fix", "per integration-patterns"), or the authoring agent. A reader at HEAD with only this file open must understand it.
- **Comments never name** customer orgs, the source integration a pattern was copied from, or observation dates — those leak or rot. The ban is on customers: naming the integration's own vendor inside its own files is normal. Rich rationale (customer, pattern source, load-bearing dates) lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Exception: vendor/3PL support-contact lines inside `support()` — naming contacts is that method's job.
- **Raise, don't `assert`.** Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` exception helpers), never `assert` — asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status or origin. `assert` belongs in tests only.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
crawler: resume from where the crawl stopped, without the overlap

A resumed crawl (the scheduler using current_crawl_start, or a sync job with
latest_data) moved its start back by the overlap again, so each restart walked the
start and latest_data back another overlap, and a stored page token no longer matched
the query that made it. The scheduler now marks resumes with a message header and the
crawler skips the overlap for them. current_crawl_start stores the start the page was
actually fetched from. Drops the latest_data clamp: a next_start inside the overlap is
how far the crawl got, so latest_data moves there and the drain waits on it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01PKbHKDKFv2Zx2QZ44FRumt
EOF

Known gap: `cancel_order` still does the bare bracket lookup with no fallback — same latent `KeyError`. Fix when next touching that path.
+### Package shipping_method / carrier: the shipment's, not the order's

+Mapping: order-level `shipping_method_*` / `carrier_*` use the order's `shipping_service` / `shipping_carrier` (what was requested); each package uses its shipment's own `shipping_service` / `shipping_carrier`, through the same table lookup and fallback.

+Why: rate-shop methods like `SELECTSHIP` / `EXPEDITED` are resolved to a real carrier at ship time, and DCL records that only on the shipment. Copying the order's values onto packages showed the requested method instead of what shipped.
+Evidence: Pylon #6306 (DietDirect), order `112-6492418-2020239` / `SO-63765`, shipment `4872904`: order `SELECTSHIP` / `EXPEDITED`, eFactory shipment `ONTRAC` / `GROUND`, tracking `D10017733141690`.
Three observed null-list shapes in the `orders` response, each handled distinctly:
join to any product from `get_products`, and there is no endpoint to enumerate or enrich
these products. This is a Squarespace API limitation, not something we can resolve; the
real `productId` is still the most faithful value to emit.
+### Digital products: one row, priced from the product
+`DIGITAL` products have no `variants`, only product-level `pricing` and `digitalGood`
+(vendor spec "Retrieve all products"). `get_products` emits the product row alone with
+`price` from that `pricing`; `sku` and `inventory` stay `None` because the API has neither.
+- **`modifiedAfter` / `modifiedBefore` do not match the returned `modifiedOn`.** Probe: all
+  125 products had `modifiedOn` on or after 2026-08-26, yet a 2026-08-26 to 2026-08-28
+  window matched 0. Open question for Squarespace: which timestamp the filter compares.

Client-side matching also could not work at all on a fast-moving sku. **`GET /api/v2/items/{id}/transactions` serves at most the item's last 10,000 transactions** and returns `500 {"error":"Item History only goes back 10000 transactions. If you need more comprehensive historical data, please use the CSV export."}` once paging goes past that. Scanning the whole history therefore died on any item with more than 10,000 rows — at `per_page=250`, page 42 onward. `whiplash_request` maps 5xx to a retriable `RetryException`, so the crawl retried twice and then failed, with no connection error recorded (a retry is neither a credential nor a permission error). That wedged `get_inbound_shipments` for two connections until the server-side filter replaced the scan (TRA-2500). The filter also collapses ~42 calls per busy item into one.

- **No synthesized fallback, and no merge with what's stored.** The per-item fetch returns every transaction the item has for this shipnotice, so `receipts` is rebuilt from it each crawl and `[]` means nothing has been received yet. `get_receipts_from_received_quantity`, the `previous_receipts` argument, and the `InboundShipment(self).batch_get_resources` prefetch that fed it are gone from the inbound crawl. Real transaction ids will not match the stored synthesized ones, so stored rows are replaced outright on the next crawl — no migration code, self-healing. `arrived_date` changes on existing receipts from crawl time to real arrival time, and receipt `id`s change.

- **Verified against prod, Aug 2026.** The sandbox still fails TLS, so this was read through the prod connections during TRA-2500. All three of the originally-open assumptions hold: the transaction row carries `shipnotice_id`; `quantity` is the running balance and `change` is the delta, so `change` is the received amount (which is what `format_inbound_shipment` already reads); and the endpoint paginates on the same `per_page` / `page` pair as the rest of the API. Sample row: `{"id":536066592,"item_id":25358696,"shipnotice_id":31912773,"description":"Stock moved from (pending) to (external)","quantity":7,"change":1,"created_at":"2026-07-08T14:46:53.000-04:00"}`.

aiTitle: Crawler overlap and pagination resume bug

input.command:
gh pr view 6292 --json body --jq .body > $TMPDIR/old.md && sed -n '/<!-- ship-on-merge -->/,$p' $TMPDIR/old.md > $TMPDIR/tail.md && cat > $TMPDIR/body.md <<'EOF'
The crawler moves the start back by the overlap, then checked `next_start` against the start from before that. A resumed crawl also moved its start back again. So with a 9:00 to 10:00 crawl and a 60 minute overlap, a `next_start` of 8:30 failed the crawl. A crawl that died and resumed from 8:30 then queried from 7:30, walking the start and `latest_data` back an hour on every restart. It also queried from a different start than the one that made its page token.

Now the overlap applies only to a fresh crawl. A resume picks up exactly where the crawl stopped, whether it continues in the same task or restarts from the scheduler.

- `celery_tasks/crawler.py`: `raw_start_str`/`raw_start_dt` is the start the task was given, and `start_time_str`/`start_time_dt` is where the loop starts (the overlap applied only if this isn't a resume). `current_start_dt` moves forward with each `next_start`. `next_start` is checked against `current_start_dt`, the start the integration was actually given.
- A resume is marked with a `resuming` message header, the same way `enqueued_at` is sent, so a worker on older code ignores it. The scheduler sets it when it starts from `current_crawl_start`. The sync job scheduler sets it when the job has a `latest_data`, and now resumes from that even if it's before the requested start.
- `current_crawl_start` stores the start the page was actually fetched from, overlap included, so the resume reproduces the query behind the stored token.
- `latest_data` can step back into the overlap (8:30 after a 9:00 start). That is how far the crawl got. The next crawl re-reads that bit, which is harmless.
- ShipStation `get_orders`: removed `start_without_overlap`, which recomputed the start without the overlap to satisfy the old check.
- Linked refresh now gets the start of the whole crawl instead of the last window's start.

Crawls resuming right after deploy were saved with the old `current_crawl_start`, the start without the overlap. They resume from that start once, not from the start their token came from.

Local tests can't reach the dev database from this machine (the same errors happen on `main`), so CI runs the suite. The new tests cover: a `next_start` inside the overlap, a resume that skips the overlap, the scheduler and sync job scheduler marking resumes, and a sync job resuming from before its requested start.

I've folded the resume fix into #6292 and pushed it, rebased on `main`: https://github.com/trackstarhq/pokedex/pull/6292. The tests haven't run yet. They still can't reach the dev database from this machine, so CI will run the full suite.

In your example (9 to 10 AM, one-hour overlap), the first query starts at 8. A `next_start` of 8:30 moves `latest_data` to 8:30. Whether the crawl carries on in the same task or dies and the scheduler restarts it, it picks up from exactly 8:30, not 7:30.

**What changed**
- **Resumes are flagged.** The scheduler adds a `resuming` message header when it starts from `current_crawl_start`. The sync job scheduler adds it when the job already has a `latest_data`. It works like `enqueued_at`: a worker still on the old code ignores it.
- **No overlap on a resume.** When the flag is set, the crawler doesn't subtract the overlap.
- **`current_crawl_start` stores the start the page was actually fetched from**, overlap included (8 AM, not 9). A resume then repeats the exact query that produced the stored page token.
- **`latest_data_dt` is gone.** `latest_data` is set to `next_start` and the drain waits on it, the same as `main`. The value changes (9:00 to 8:30), so the drain can no longer return early, which was Greptile's point. I didn't reply to the Greptile comment.
- **Sync jobs resume from their own `latest_data`** rather than `max(requested_start, latest_data)`. With 8:30 before a 9 AM requested start, the `max` would otherwise have skipped half an hour.
- `message_enqueued_at` is now `message_header(request, key)` and handles both headers.

**One case I left alone.** You said to skip the overlap when a page token is resuming. I did that only when the token comes with a `current_crawl_start` (any resource that stores crawl params always saves both together). Returns, inventory ledger, warehouses and carrier invoices store a token but no crawl params, and resume from `latest_data`. Their `latest_data` can't move during a crawl, because `next_start` requires crawl params. So applying the overlap again recreates their original 8 AM query exactly, and skipping it would pair an 8 AM token with a 9 AM query.

**Deploy note (also in the PR):** crawls that are partway through at deploy time have a `current_crawl_start` saved by the old code, which is the start without the overlap. Each of those resumes once from a start that doesn't match its token, then everything lines up.

**Tests**
- Updated `test_first_crawl`: `current_crawl_start` now includes the overlap.
- Updated the test for a `next_start` inside the overlap: `latest_data` moves to 8:30.
- Added a test that a fresh crawl applies the overlap and a resumed one doesn't.
- Added checks that the scheduler and sync job scheduler set `resuming`.
- Added a test for a sync job resuming from before its requested start.

Everything we'd paused is now in the PR, so I deleted the note I saved earlier.

content.text:
We can. I used a header because of the one existing precedent: `enqueue_crawl_task` sends `enqueued_at` as a header, with the comment "a header, not an argument, so a worker on older code just ignores it" (`celery_tasks/crawler.py`).

The issue is deploy order. The scheduler lambda and the crawler workers ship as separate services. If the scheduler goes out first and sends `resuming=True` as a task argument, an old worker's `crawl_task` fails with `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'resuming'`. The same happens to messages already queued if the crawler is rolled back. A header avoids both problems because older code never reads it.

That risk is small, though:
- Only resumed crawls would carry the argument. If it's only sent when true, fresh crawls have the same shape as today.
- A failed task never starts, so the scheduler re-enqueues it on its next pass once the grace period is up. It fixes itself after the deploy finishes.
- Shipping `crawler` and `crawler-protected` before `scheduler` and `sync-job-scheduler` avoids it altogether.

An argument is also the more honest design. It sits in the task signature, where anyone reading `crawl_task` sees it. A header is effectively a hidden parameter that you only find through `message_header`. Two more reasons to prefer the argument:
- Local `yarn crawl` and tests could pass it directly, without `apply(headers=...)`.
- `enqueue_crawl_task_synced` wouldn't need to switch from `.delay` to `apply_async`.

If you're fine shipping the crawler first, or with a few resumed crawls failing and being re-enqueued during the deploy, I'd switch to an argument. That means:
- a `resuming=False` parameter on `crawl_task`, `crawl_task_protected`, `crawl_task_synced` and `_execute_crawl_task`
- the scheduler and sync job scheduler passing it
- dropping the `resuming` header

`enqueued_at` would stay a header. It's metadata about the message, not an input to the crawl. Want me to switch it?

content.text:
`resuming` is now a task argument, and I've pushed it to #6292 (rebased on `main`). As before, the tests can't run from this machine, so CI will be the first real run.

- **Task arguments:** `crawl_task`, `crawl_task_protected` and `crawl_task_synced` take `resuming=False` and pass it to `_execute_crawl_task`. The overlap check now reads the argument instead of a header.
- **Scheduler:** it sends `resuming` through `enqueue_crawl_task`, which already passes extra keyword arguments on to the task.
- **Sync jobs:** `enqueue_crawl_task_synced` is back on `.delay(..., resuming=resuming)`.
- **Header removed:** `enqueued_at` is the only header again. `message_header` is back to `message_enqueued_at`, and I reverted its test.
- **Tests:** the fresh-vs-resume test calls `crawl_task(..., resuming=...)` directly.

**Deploy order matters more than I said last time.** I told you only resumed crawls would carry the new argument. In fact the scheduler sends it on every crawl, including `resuming=False`. So if the schedulers ship before the workers, every crawl fails until the workers update, not just resumes. The scheduler then re-enqueues them, so it recovers either way. The PR body now says to ship `crawler` and `crawler-protected` before `scheduler` and `sync-job-scheduler`.

content.text:
That's on purpose, but the reason isn't visible in the code. `enqueue_args` is the positional argument list sent to `crawl_task`, and `resuming` can't be added to the end of it.

`crawl_task`'s positional order after `page_token` is `force, local_submit, no_heartbeat, resuming`. A tuple with 8 items would put `resuming` into `force`. So I pass it as a keyword argument instead: `process_connection` adds it next to `enqueue_args` in the `tasks_to_enqueue` tuple, and the handler calls `enqueue_crawl_task(*enqueue_args, connection_errors=..., resuming=resuming)`.

To really put it inside `enqueue_args`, the options are:

1. **Turn `enqueue_args` into a dict of keyword arguments** (`connection_row=`, `start_time_str=`, `resuming=`, …). This is the cleanest result: the log list and the args become the same thing, and nothing depends on position. The cost is that `enqueue_crawl_task` reads `args[0]`, `args[2]` and `args[4]`, and about a dozen scheduler tests assert on `call[0][n]`, so all of those change.
2. **Move `resuming` right after `page_token` in the task signature.** Don't do this. Messages already in the queue send `force` in that position, so they'd be read as `resuming`.
3. **Fill in the defaults** (`..., page_token, False, False, False, resuming`). It's short, but it looks like the scheduler is choosing `force`, `local_submit` and `no_heartbeat`, which it isn't.

I'd go with 1 if you want `resuming` to live with the other arguments. Otherwise the current version is fine and just needs a comment explaining why it sits next to `enqueue_args` rather than inside it. Which do you want?

    return offsets[lineno - 1] + col
inserts = []

    if not isinstance(node, ast.Call):
        continue
    f = node.func
    if not isinstance(f, ast.Attribute):

    kw = [k.arg for k in node.keywords]
    if f.attr in ("crawl_task", "crawl_task_protected") and len(node.args) == 7 and "resuming" not in kw:

        a = node.args[5]
        inserts.append((off(a.end_lineno, a.end_col_offset), ", None, False"))
    elif f.attr == "apply" and isinstance(f.value, ast.Attribute) and f.value.attr == "crawl_task":
        args_kw = next(k for k in node.keywords if k.arg == "args")
        a = args_kw.value.elts[-1]
        inserts.append((off(a.end_lineno, a.end_col_offset), ", False"))
for pos, text in sorted(inserts, reverse=True):
    src = src[:pos] + text + src[pos:]
open(p, "w").write(src)
print(len(inserts))
EOF

Each ship notice has a `PartnerInformation` with `BillToShipToInformation="SF"` whose `IdentificationCode` is the DC id zero-padded (`03` Mesquite, `04` St. Peters). A shipment uses its own notice; the order uses its first notice and stays `None` until DM sends one.

- **Order write `warehouse_id` → `ShippingInformation.ForceDC`.** Optional. Without it DM ships from the DC closest to the customer, and DM warned forcing a DC can lengthen delivery (email, 9/25). The write check (`validate_warehouse_id`) passes when the read has no DC yet and otherwise requires it to match.

- **`required_ship_date` is write-only; its write validation always passes.** `create_order` sends it as `ShipWindowEndDate`, but `GetOrders` has no ship-window field (its `SalesOrder` returns order type, status, totals, PO numbers, addresses and lines only), so the read stays `IntegrationNotImplemented` and a strict compare would log a false mismatch on every order sent with a ship date. Seen on KBS order SO-05899 (Pylon 6260).

content.text:
`resuming` is now a required argument right after `page_token`, and every enqueue sends the task arguments by name. I pushed it to #6292, rebased on `main`, at `5e6983ca1`. The tests still haven't run: the dev database isn't reachable from this machine, so CI will be the first run. Locally I only checked that everything compiles, the lint counts are unchanged, and the task signatures print as expected.

**Changes**
- **Signatures:** `crawl_task`, `crawl_task_protected`, `crawl_task_synced` and `_execute_crawl_task` now go `..., page_token, resuming, force=False, ...`. There's no default for `resuming`. In `crawl_task_synced`, `page_token` is also required now, because a required argument can't follow one with a default.
- **Enqueue arguments sent by name:**
  - The scheduler's `enqueue_args` is a dict keyed by parameter name, `resuming` included, and `enqueue_crawl_task(task_kwargs, connection_errors=None)` sends it as `apply_async(kwargs=...)`.
  - The API force sync (`utils/api.py`) and the Lambda crawler build the same dict, with `resuming: False`.
  - `enqueue_crawl_task_synced` sends its arguments by name.
  - The tasks pass everything on to `_execute_crawl_task` by name.
- **Local crawls:** `scripts/crawl.py` passes `False`, so a local run always applies the overlap.
- **Tests:**
  - The 33 direct task calls in `crawl_test.py` pass `resuming`.
  - The scheduler and API tests read the enqueue arguments by key (`["function_name"]`, `["start_time_str"]`) instead of by position.

**Deploy:** sending by name removes the risk that a value lands in the wrong parameter (for example `resuming=True` being read as `force` by an older worker). A mismatched sender and worker now just fail with a `TypeError`. The catch is that neither ship order is clean any more, since every message now carries a required `resuming`. Crawls queued across the deploy will fail until both sides are updated, then the scheduler re-enqueues them. The PR body now says to ship the crawler workers and the schedulers together.

**Greptile:** the Greptile MCP needs you to sign in again (`/mcp`), so I retriggered the review by commenting `@greptileai` on the PR: https://github.com/trackstarhq/pokedex/pull/6292#issuecomment-5915928911

content.text:
**#6292: crawler: resume from where the crawl stopped, and check next_start against the start the integration was given**

- **Bug 1:** the crawler checked `next_start` against the start from before the overlap was applied. A `next_start` inside the overlap (8:30 for a 9:00 start with a one-hour overlap) failed the crawl, even though the integration had been asked for data from 8:00.
- **Bug 2:** a resumed crawl applied the overlap again. A crawl that died and resumed from 8:30 queried from 7:30, moving the start and `latest_data` back an hour on every restart. The query also no longer matched the one that produced the stored page token.
- **Start variables:**
  - `raw_start_str`/`raw_start_dt` is the start the task was given.
  - `start_time_str`/`start_time_dt` mirror each other and are where the loop begins: the raw start minus the overlap, or no overlap on a resume.
  - `current_start_dt` moves forward with each `next_start`.
- **`next_start` check:** it's now compared against `current_start_dt`, the start the integration actually received.
- **`latest_data`:** set to `next_start` even when that's inside the overlap, since that's how far the crawl got. The submit drain waits on that value, which resolves Greptile's early-return comment.
- **`current_crawl_start`:** stores the start the page was actually fetched from, overlap included, so a resume repeats the query behind the stored token.
- **`resuming` argument:**
  - It's a required argument right after `page_token` on `crawl_task`, `crawl_task_protected` and `crawl_task_synced`, and the crawler skips the overlap when it's true.
  - The scheduler sets it when it starts from `current_crawl_start`. The sync job scheduler sets it when the job has a `latest_data`, and now resumes from that even if it's before the requested start.
- **Arguments sent by name:** every enqueue (scheduler, sync job scheduler, API force sync, Lambda crawler) sends the task arguments by name. The scheduler's `enqueue_args` is now a dict. A mismatched sender and worker fail with a `TypeError` instead of putting a value in the wrong parameter.
- **Only a `current_crawl_start` resume skips the overlap.** Resources that store a page token without crawl params (returns, inventory ledger, warehouses, carrier invoices) resume from `latest_data`, which can't move during their crawl, so applying the overlap again reproduces their original query.
- **ShipStation:** removed the `start_without_overlap` workaround in `get_orders`.
- **Linked refresh:** now gets the start of the whole crawl instead of the last window's start.
- **Deploy:**
  - Ship the crawler workers and the schedulers together. Crawls queued across the deploy fail once, and the scheduler re-enqueues them.
  - Crawls already partway through resume once from the old `current_crawl_start`, which doesn't include the overlap.
- **Tests:** added tests for a `next_start` inside the overlap, a fresh vs resumed crawl start, the scheduler and sync job scheduler setting `resuming`, and a sync job resuming from before its requested start. Existing tests now read the enqueue arguments by name.
- **Verification:** local tests can't reach the dev database, so CI runs the full suite. On the earlier commit, the only CI failures were live vendor tests (i-fulfilment timeouts, oia-global, tps, mabang, ffe). I've retriggered Greptile on the latest commit.

aiTitle: Crawler overlap and pagination resume bug

content.text:
I'd add an optional `resuming` key that defaults to `false`, and make it required when `page_token` is set. I wouldn't infer it from the token, because the token doesn't determine it in either direction:

- **A token with `resuming: false`:** returns, inventory ledger, warehouses and carrier invoices store a token but no crawl params. They resume from `latest_data`, and the overlap has to be applied again to reproduce the query that produced the token. If a token implied `true`, this case would query from the wrong start.
- **`resuming: true` with no token:** a resource with crawl params that died just after a `next_start` window drained has `current_crawl_start` set and no token. A rule based on the token would miss this case.

Requiring `resuming` on every run would also work, but most local crawls are fresh and would carry a key that is always `false`. That's friction without any safety gain.

This fits our style:
- **No `.get` default:** the script already reads optional keys with `if "page_token" in params:`. `resuming` would follow the same pattern with `False` as its starting value. The `.get` rule is about vendor responses, and a config key that's normally absent is the documented exception.
- **Fail loudly on the ambiguous case:** a token with no `resuming` key raises, because that's the only case where the value can't be guessed safely. Something like: `crawl.json has a page_token, so set "resuming": true if it came from current_crawl_start (the start already includes the overlap), or false if it came from latest_data`.

I'd also update the help text in `scripts/crawl.py` and the table in `run-scripts/guides/crawl.md`.

There's a related gap in the script. Its sync-job path always starts from the job's `requested_start_time`. The sync job scheduler now resumes from the job's `latest_data` with `resuming=True`. With `"resuming": true`, the script should do the same, or a local run of a resumed job starts from a different place than production would.

Want me to add both to #6292?

lines: - ShipHero's gateway returns HTML 502s and 504s when busy, so `response.json()` throws on them. `shiphero_request` treats a 502, or a 504 on a read, as a `RetryException` (60s back-off, retried) — a 504 is load-dependent, not a permanently slow query (the same request ran 12s–186s across attempts; TRA-2435, PR #5294). A 504 on a write fails fast: the timed-out mutation may already have landed, and retrying could duplicate it. Small page sizes (see the `get_products` entry) remain the first defense against triggering 504s at all.

- `return_create` can save the return yet send back a response with only `id`, `legacy_id`, `account_id`, `status` and `created_at` filled in; every other field (including `line_items`) is null and `errors` holds `Expected int-compatible resource key, got NoneType`. `create_return` detects `line_items: None`, reads the return back with `get_return`, and keeps the mutation errors in `additional_fields.errors`. If that read fails, the error names the created return id so a caller doesn't retry into a duplicate. The error never appeared on return reads. Evidence: connection `b7c2efa95a4e44a2825586a655a96fb4`, 19 of ~2,200 creates (e.g. return `UmV0dXJuOjE0MTk0MzQ3`); Pylon #6276.

+- Since Sep 16 2026, `/auth/token` answers password logins sent from our AWS servers with `401 {"message": "Unauthorized"}`, even for credentials that get a token from anywhere else (the identical `requests` call from a laptop returns 200). Almost every install failed with "Invalid ShipHero credentials" until this was found. `get_integration_secret` therefore sends the login through one of the Browserbase ISP exit IPs (`BROWSER_EXTERNAL_PROXY_IPS`, proxy login in the `creds/browserbase` secret), trying each until one connects. Verified with our sandbox user daniel+2@trackstarhq.com: 401 from `lambda-api-prod`, 200 direct from a laptop and through the proxy IPs. `/auth/refresh` still works from AWS, so crawls go direct. ShipHero support has been asked why our IPs are rejected; drop the proxy if they lift it.

content.text:
I've made both fixes and pushed them to #6292 as `b8008839c`, rebased on `main`. I haven't run `yarn crawl` with the new keys; I only checked that the script compiles.

**`crawl.json` `resuming` key (`scripts/crawl.py`)**
- It's read the same way as the other optional keys (`if "resuming" in params:`) and defaults to `false`.
- If there's a `page_token` but no `resuming`, the script raises: `crawl.json has a page_token, so set "resuming": true if it came from current_crawl_start (the start already includes the overlap), or false if it came from latest_data`.
- It's passed through to `crawl_task` and `crawl_task_synced`, replacing the hardcoded `False`.

**Sync-job path:** with `job_id` and `"resuming": true`, the script now starts from the job's `latest_data` instead of `requested_start_time`, matching the sync job scheduler. It indexes `job["latest_data"]` directly, so a job with no `latest_data` fails loudly.

**Docs:** I added `resuming` to the script's help text, and to the example and field table in `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/crawl.md`.

The PR body has a line for the new `yarn crawl` behaviour. I didn't retrigger Greptile for this push; I can if you want.

The code is done. The one thing left is the deploy: nothing has shipped yet, because no stage or service was ticked in the PR's ship block before the merge.

**Deploy.** Because `resuming` is now a required argument, these need to go out together, for dev and then prod:
- `crawler` and `crawler-protected` (the task signatures)
- `scheduler` and `sync-job-scheduler` (they now send arguments by name, including `resuming`)
- `lambda-crawler` (`lambda_handlers/crawler.py` changed)
- `api` (the force sync in `utils/api.py` sends the new dict)

Remember that shipping `crawler` kills running crawls. They restart once their heartbeat goes stale, which takes up to 10 minutes.

**After deploy, check Datadog for:**
- `TypeError`s from `crawl_task` about `resuming`. Crawls queued across the deploy should hit this once, then get re-enqueued. They should stop after one scheduler pass.
- Crawls that were partway through at deploy. They resume once from the old `current_crawl_start`, which didn't include the overlap. That only matters for integrations with offset or opaque page tokens, and it happens once.

**CI and review: nothing to act on.**
- The final run had 29 failures, all live vendor tests: ShipHero credentials, oia-global, tps, mabang, dcl, gobolt, ongoing, shipfusion, whiplash cleanup.
